bullets: How far a bus travelling at 60 km/h goes in 2.5 hours, using distance = speed × time
slides.heading: Rate and speed: d = s × t
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we meet speed as a rate - what 60 km/h really means, and how to turn a speed and a time into a distance - and by the end you will be able to explain why a speed on its own is never a distance.

bullets: Read speed as distance per hour: 60 km/h means 60 km in every hour
Find distance by multiplying: distance = speed × time
Work out 60 km/h for 2.5 hours: 60 × 2.5 = 150 km
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A classmate says a bus travelling at 60 km/h has already gone 60 km after only half an hour
Is that possible? What does the 60 in 60 km/h really count?
slides.heading: Has the bus already gone 60 km?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: has the bus gone 60 km after half an hour, or must something be wrong? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s3 settles this exactly.

bullets: Speed is a rate: it tells the distance covered in one unit of time, so 60 km/h is 60 km in each hour
Distance, speed and time are linked: distance = speed × time, so the time always matters
slides.heading: Speed is a rate: distance per unit of time
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: a speed counts distance per hour, and only a speed together with a time gives a distance.

bullets: A bus at 60 km/h covers 60 km in the first hour, 120 km after 2 hours and 180 km after 3 hours
Each hour adds the same 60 km: the distance grows by the speed every hour
slides.heading: Speed is distance per hour
slides.notes: Point at the distance chips as they appear and narrate: 60 km after one hour, 120 km after two, 180 km after three - the same 60 km landing every hour.

bullets: Multiply speed by time: 60 × 2.5 = 150 km
Check by parts: 60 km in hour one, 60 km in hour two, and half of 60 km - 30 km - in the half hour: 60 + 60 + 30 = 150 km
slides.heading: 60 km/h for 2.5 hours
slides.notes: Narrate the journey slowly: the bus passes 60 km, then 120 km, then a shorter half-hour step lands it on 150 km. The bar underneath grows by a full 60 km block per hour and a half block for the half hour.

bullets: Careful - the trap is reading 60 km/h as a distance travelled, whatever the time
After half an hour at 60 km/h the bus has gone 60 × 1/2 = 30 km, not 60 km
slides.heading: Watch out: speed is not distance
slides.notes: Hold the claim up against the road: the bus stops at the half-hour mark, 30 km along, while the 60 km answer sits far ahead of it - half the time means half the distance.

bullets: To find distance: distance = speed × time - cover the d in the triangle to see the working
Flip the formula either way: speed = distance ÷ time and time = distance ÷ speed
slides.heading: The takeaway
slides.notes: Land the whole family in one breath: distance, speed and time are one family - multiply speed by time for distance, and divide to flip the formula for speed or for time.

bullets: Work the distance in one step: distance = speed × time, so 60 × 2.5 = 150 km
Sanity-check by hours: 60 km + 60 km + 30 km for the half hour = 150 km
slides.heading: Worked example: 60 km/h for 2.5 hours
slides.notes: Talk through the multiplication slowly as in scene s2 and name each part as you write it; say: checking by hours - 60, 60, then half of 60 - keeps the working honest.

bullets: A cyclist rides at 12 km/h for 3 hours. How far does she go? Use distance = speed × time
A car travels at 80 km/h for half an hour. How far does it go, and why is the answer not 80 km?
slides.heading: Your turn: find the distance
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the multiplication first, then on the exact sentence they used to explain why half an hour cannot give 80 km.

bullets: On your own: a train travels at 90 km/h for 2 hours - how far does it go?
Explain in one sentence why a speed on its own is not a distance
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the distance = speed × time working in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about distance per hour in your second.
